newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Ethiopia says financial sector underdeveloped.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopia says financial sector underdeveloped.

text.p: Ethiopia said on Monday economic reforms had produced significant results but its banking and financial sectors were largely underdeveloped.

Deputy Prime Minister Kassu Ilala told African finance ministers and officials from lending institutions meeting in the capital Addis Ababa that the Horn of African country was committed to creating an environment to foster investment.
"Our banking and financial structures are still undeveloped and financial instruments remain narrow in scope," he said.

Ethiopia is classified as one of the least developed and most heavily indebted countries. It has obtained a total of $380 million debt reduction under the so-called "Naples terms", which allow reduction on debt repayments of up to 67 percent.
Ethiopia expects a further $167 million of its total $4.4 billion external debt to be restructured in the near future under the same Naples terms, Kassu said.
An additional $256 million of Ethiopian debt has been retired through a commercial buy-back programme, using funds from the World Bank, Britain and the Netherlands.

Ethiopia successfuly implemented the first stages of economic reforms starting in 1992/93 under the supervision of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, leading to average gross domestic product growth of 7.6 percent a year, according to finance ministry figures.
Ethiopia has embarked on the second phase of reforms from 1996/97 which it sees leading to an average economic growth of 8.0 percent, said Finance Minister Sufian Ahmed.
Sufian said average inflation in the 1992/93 to 1994/95 period was 6.3 percent and there were indications that it would decline more during the second phase of strict reforms.

"We are determined to make more efforts to improve the dispersion of financial infrastructure, deepen financial instruments and strengthen further the sector's capacity to mobilise and efficiently allocate resources," Kassu said.
He added that Ethiopia had licensed privately-owned commercial banks along with other financial institutions such as insurance companies as part of financial sector reform.
He said the government also eliminated preferential credit treatment for state-owned companies, helping to speed private sector expansion.
Other reforms included weekly currency auctions and the launch of debt instruments such as government treasury bills.
Kassu said Ethiopia expected to be one of the candidates to benefit from the new Heavily Indebted Poor Countries initiative which targets the globe's poorest countries.
Uganda is expected to the the first beneficiary.
